title: Pawn-step timing: one step or two
outcomes: Explains that a pawn still on its starting square can spend its moves as one step or two, and so changes who runs out of spare moves
Finds the pawn step that keeps a win in a locked-pawn ending
Tells a position where the count decides from one where no pawn has a spare move

steps.text: The lesson *Spare moves: who runs out first?* counts free squares between pawns. A pawn on its **starting square** adds a choice: it can step once or twice, so its owner can change the count. Timing means choosing the step that leaves the opponent without a spare move first. These positions are our own reconstructions, checked in the tablebase, not copies of a book's diagrams.

steps.caption: White to move. The f-pawns are locked; the a-pawns are free to move. The single step a3 wins, the double step a4 does not.

line.say: The pawn takes one step, keeping a second step in reserve.
White's pawn steps up and the two a-pawns now face each other.
Black has no pawn move left; the king moves.

steps.text: **Conditions.** The count only decides while both kings are tied to their squares and the pawns are locked. It is a heuristic, not a law: in the first pair below both sides lose if they must move. Check three things before you push: is a king free, how many squares lie between the flank pawns, and which pawn still has the choice of one step or two?

steps.title: One free square fewer
steps.prompt: Black to move. In the first position, Black wins. In the second, White's pawn is still on its starting square. Predict each.

steps.title: Who must move, and one pawn step
steps.prompt: Pawns locked on d5 and d6. First: White to move with both h-pawns on their starting squares. Then the same with Black to move. Then Black's h-pawn one step further. Predict each.
Before each answer: did you ask whether a king was free and which pawn still had two ways to move? Which of the two did you forget?
